lesson.title: One Bone Plan, Many Jobs: Homologous Structures
lesson.summary: Homologous structures share the same underlying architecture and developmental origin because they were inherited from a common ancestor, even when natural selection has since modified them to serve very different functions.
lesson.body:
A homologous structure is a structure that two or more species share because they inherited it, in modified form, from a common ancestor, not because it currently serves the same purpose in each species. The key word is inherited. Homology is about shared origin, not shared job. Two structures can look and function completely differently today and still be homologous, as long as they trace back to the same structure in a shared ancestor.

The vertebrate forelimb introduced in the last chapter is the textbook case. A human arm grasps and manipulates tools. A whale's flipper steers and stabilizes an entirely aquatic body. A bat's wing generates lift for powered flight. A cat's foreleg supports weight and enables running. A bird's wing also flies, but along a completely separate branch of the vertebrate family tree from bats. All five are built from the same underlying bone plan, one long bone, then two, then a cluster of wrist bones, then digits, just reshaped, resized, and in some cases fused or reduced, by natural selection acting differently in each lineage after they split from their shared ancestor. That single shared skeletal blueprint, repurposed five different ways, only makes sense as inheritance with modification. If each of these limbs had arisen completely independently to solve its own functional problem, there would be no reason to expect them to share the exact same underlying bone arrangement.

This is why homology is such strong evidence for evolution specifically, and not just for the general idea that similar structures exist in nature: it explains a pattern, the same underlying architecture turning up again and again across very different functions, that has a natural, testable cause. Common descent predicts exactly this pattern. Closely related species should share more homologous detail than distantly related ones, since less evolutionary time has passed since they shared a common ancestor. That prediction holds up consistently across the anatomical record, and, as later chapters in this unit will show, it holds up independently in the embryological and molecular records too.

It is worth being precise about what homology does and does not claim. Homologous structures do not need to look alike, and they do not need to do the same job. What they need to share is underlying structural and developmental origin traceable to a common ancestor. This is exactly the opposite of the pattern covered in the next chapter, where structures that do look alike and do the same job turn out to have arisen completely independently. Keeping these two categories straight, same origin regardless of function for homologous structures, versus same function regardless of origin for analogous structures, is one of the more commonly confused, and more important, distinctions in evolutionary biology.
